rules.title: Possessive Pronouns vs Possessive Adjectives
rules.concept: Distinguish possessive adjectives from possessive pronouns. Possessive adjectives: my, our, your, his/her/its, their (used before a noun). Possessive pronouns: mine, ours, yours, his/hers, theirs (used alone, without a noun). Also note: 'its' is a possessive adjective while 'it's' is a contraction of pronoun + verb (it is/it has). For a compound subject like 'You and Rohan', use 'your'; for 'You and I', use 'our'; for 'He and I', use 'our'.

examples.sentence: I have decided that I won't work at yours company anymore.
Their is the best offer that you can get so you should not think much.
I can't buy this car because it's cost is way out of my budget.
examples.correction: Use 'its' instead of 'it's'. 'Its' is a possessive adjective, whereas 'it's' is pronoun + verb.

examples.sentence: You and Rohan should not waste his time wandering here and there.
You and I have done my best to make her happy.
He and I will not leave any stone unturned to complete ours assignment.

rules.title: Reflexive Pronouns after certain verbs
rules.concept: Use a reflexive pronoun (myself, ourselves, yourself, yourselves, himself, herself, itself, themselves) after these verbs: absent, present, adapt, adjust, acquit, exert, apply, hurt, prostrate, submit, resign, reconcile, introduce, avail, amuse, enjoy, satisfy, avenge, pride, etc. The reflexive pronoun must agree with the subject in number.

examples.sentence: He introduced to the Chairman as the General Secretary of the party.
examples.correction: The verb 'introduced' needs an object, so add the reflexive pronoun 'himself' before 'to'.

examples.sentence: He prostrated before his master who taught him when he was in school.
examples.correction: 'Prostrated' is a transitive verb and needs an object, so use 'himself' after 'prostrated'.

examples.sentence: The minister and his cabinet members absented himself from the meeting.

rules.title: Each / Either / Neither + of
rules.concept: Structure: Each/Either/Neither + of + plural noun + singular verb + singular pronoun/adjective.

examples.sentence: Each of the boys have completed their assignment.
examples.correction: Use 'has' instead of 'have' and use 'his' instead of 'their'.

examples.sentence: Each of these 5 students have worked very hard on this project.
They told me that neither of them were present there when the accident happened.

rules.title: Out of class comparison / 'that of' concept
rules.concept: When comparing, compare like with like. Use 'that of' (or 'those of', or an apostrophe form) so that the same noun is compared on both sides, rather than comparing a quality with a person or place.

examples.sentence: The air of Delhi is more polluted than Mumbai.
examples.correction: Delhi's air must be compared with Mumbai's air, so use 'that of' where 'that' stands for 'air': ...than that of Mumbai.

examples.sentence: The maximum speed of my car is way more than yours.
examples.correction: The speed of one car must be compared with the speed of the other car, so use 'that of': 'that of yours' = the speed of your car.

examples.sentence: Rohit and Rahul both are my friends, but Rohit's sense of humour is better than Rahul.
examples.correction: Rohit's sense of humour must be compared with Rahul's sense of humour. There is no need to repeat the noun 'sense of humour'; simply add an apostrophe to Rahul, so use 'Rahul's'.

rules.title: Uses of Relative Pronouns
rules.concept: Who/whom are used for human beings (who as subject, whom as object); which is used for things and for clauses; that is used to give emphasis with human beings or things (especially after superlatives, 'the only', 'the same', 'the few', etc.); what is used for noun clauses.

examples.sentence: The girl who you had slapped in the class complained to the principal.
Sahil, whom just started last week, is already doing good at his new job.
The car which/who is standing in front of my house is my father's.
You have never questioned any decision of your master that is a proof of your loyalty.
examples.correction: Here the relative pronoun must refer to the whole clause. When an entire clause acts as the antecedent, the relative pronoun 'which' is used.

examples.sentence: The few people who came to my party are the only friends that I have till now.
He told me that he saw the same boy who killed your dog.
I cannot predict that might happen if you don't submit your fees on time.
You shouldn't judge a person when you don't know that he has gone through.

rules.title: Relative pronouns take the verb according to their antecedent
rules.concept: A relative pronoun takes its verb (and related pronouns) according to its antecedent. In 'one of those who...' the antecedent is plural, so use a plural verb and plural pronoun; in 'the only one of the... that...' the antecedent is 'one', so use a singular verb.

examples.sentence: He is one of those who can sacrifice his life for the country.
This novel is one of the best novels that has been written in the last 10 years.
Roshni is the only one of the girls that have scored more than 98% marks in the exam.

rules.title: Subject 'one' takes 'one's' / 'oneself'
rules.concept: If the subject is 'one', use the pronoun, adjective, etc. according to 'one' (one's, oneself) and not 'he', 'his' or 'himself'.

examples.sentence: One should respect his parents.
One should never criticize others if he not sure of his facts.
He added philosophically that one should adapt himself to the changing conditions.

rules.title: Quantifiers/Fractions + of + Noun + Verb
rules.concept: With expressions such as All, Some, Most, A lot, Lots, Plenty, and percentages or fractions (20%, 30%, 1/2, one third, two fifths), the structure is: quantifier/fraction + of + noun + verb, and the verb agrees with the noun that follows 'of'. If that noun is plural, use a plural verb; if it is singular or uncountable, use a singular verb.

examples.sentence: Some of the students was absent yesterday.
Half of the class have not completed the assignment given by the teacher.
All of the chairs was in perfect condition when I bought them from the new furniture store.

rules.title: Comparison of pronouns
rules.concept: In comparisons, keep the cases parallel: compare a subject with a subject and an object with an object. So after 'than' or 'as ... as', use the subject pronoun when the comparison is with the subject of the sentence.

examples.sentence: You are stronger than him so you can easily defeat him.
I was surprised to find that their tallest player was shorter than me.
I have told you many times that you are as smart as him.

rules.title: Objective case after certain prepositions and prepositional phrases
rules.concept: Use the objective case of the pronoun after these words: between, with, besides, including, excluding, but, like, unlike, together with, along with, as well as, and not, in addition to, rather than, accompanied by, no less than, nothing but, etc. This is because all of these words and phrases are prepositions or prepositional phrases.

examples.sentence: Between you and I, I think he is not dressed appropriately for the occasion.
I think he is a bit ungrateful, because everyone but he was happy to receive gift on Christmas.

rules.title: Position of ordinals and cardinals
rules.concept: When an ordinal (first, last, next) and a cardinal number (five, ten, two) are used together, the ordinal comes before the cardinal: 'first five', 'first ten', 'last two'.

examples.sentence: He has solved the five first questions of the exercise.
examples.correction: Use 'first five questions' instead of 'five first questions'.

examples.sentence: The policeman checked only the ten first trucks that were standing in the line.
examples.correction: Use 'first ten trucks' instead of 'ten first trucks'.

examples.sentence: 15 men went into lion's den one by one as a challenge but only the two last survived.
examples.correction: Use 'the last two' instead of 'the two last'.

rules.title: Each/Either/Neither/Every + singular noun + singular verb
rules.concept: Each, either, neither and every are followed by a singular noun and take a singular verb.

examples.sentence: Each boy of this class were called by the principal.
According to the rules set by the judges, each speaker were allowed to speak for 5 minutes.
I am going to the family function only because every cousin of mine are coming.

rules.title: Some vs any
rules.concept: Use 'some' in affirmative (positive) sentences and 'any' in negative and interrogative sentences.

examples.sentence: I don't have some/any experience of this field.
She told me that she needed any time to think about my proposal.
You all are invited to my birthday party this weekend but please don't bring some presents.

rules.title: Adjectives that cannot be intensified or compared
rules.concept: Do not use 'very', 'more' or 'most' with these absolute adjectives: impossible, universal, eternal, chief, ideal, supreme, perfect, unique, excellent, full, empty, entire, dead, free, circular, rectangular, etc.

examples.sentence: I can assure you that this school is most excellent.
I really love the area and see it as the most ideal place to get married.
Today I met a person who could communicate with animals, I guess some humans are born with the most unique talents.

rules.title: Excluding the subject from the group it is compared with
rules.concept: When a person or thing is compared with a group, that person or thing must not be included in the group. Therefore use 'all the other' or 'no other' to exclude it.

examples.sentence: Rohan is taller than all the boys of his class.
examples.correction: Use 'all the other boys' instead of 'all the boys'.

examples.sentence: Rahul, my colleague is more hardworking than all the employees of our company.
examples.correction: Use 'all the other employees' instead of 'all the employees'.

examples.sentence: Based on the stories that I read when I was child, I think no animal is as cunning as a fox.
examples.correction: Use 'I think no other animal' instead of 'I think no animal'.

rules.title: No double comparatives or superlatives
rules.concept: Do not use 'more' with comparative degree adjectives or 'most' with superlative degree adjectives. To emphasise a comparative, use 'much' or 'far'; to emphasise a superlative, use 'by far' or 'much'.

examples.sentence: He is more stronger than Ajay.
Mr. Mehta has two daughters and the younger one is more prettier than the older one.
I really like spending time with him as he is the most nicest person that I have ever met.
examples.correction: Use 'by far/much' after 'as he is' and remove 'most'.

rules.title: Confusing pairs: later/latter, farther/further, good/well, bad/ill, far/a long way, last/latest, next/nearest
rules.concept: Distinguish these commonly confused pairs: 'later' refers to time while 'latter' means the second of two things; 'farther' is used for physical distance while 'further' means 'in addition to something'; 'good' is an adjective while 'well' is an adverb; 'bad' is an adjective while 'ill' is an adverb; 'far' is used in negative and interrogative sentences while 'a long way' is used in positive (affirmative) sentences. Also distinguish 'last' from 'latest' and 'next' from 'nearest'.

examples.sentence: Of these two choices of cuisines, I would love to have the later one.
I hope it won't be a problem if we postpone this meeting to a latter date.
I wanted to discuss that topic farther, but my professor didn't have time.
My college is located further than hers yet she got a scooty and I got a bicycle.
My friend has told me that this new restaurant serves well Indian food.
I stayed up all night and prepared a lot for my meeting but it didn't go good.
When he was here last year, he was grossly bad treated by you.
Rohit has made some bad choices in life but trust me he is not an ill person.
How far/a long way is the library from your house?
He is good at shooting the ball into the net from far.

rules.title: Present participle vs past participle
rules.concept: Distinguish the present participle from the past participle when used as an adjective. The past participle describes the person who experiences the feeling (a horrified man = a frightened man), while the present participle describes the thing that causes the feeling (a horrifying man = a frightening man).

examples.sentence: He solved that confused question very easily.
He told me that he had gifted his girlfriend a very interested novel on her birthday.
I tried a lot but I could not find my losing book.

rules.title: Little / a little / the little and few / a few / the few
rules.concept: 'Little' and 'few' carry a negative sense (hardly any); 'a little' and 'a few' carry a positive sense (some); 'the little' and 'the few' refer to the whole of the small quantity or number that is available.

examples.sentence: Could you give me …… sugar?
When my friend was in trouble I offered him a little money that I had with me.
I was out of town and couldn't find a place to rest therefore I got very a little sleep last night.
He met with an accident yesterday, and the doctor advised him to rest for the few days.
The school had to cancel the debate competition as a few students participated in it.

rules.title: Correct degree of adjective
rules.concept: Use the correct degree of the adjective according to the meaning of the sentence.

examples.sentence: Rahul is stronger and wise than Mahesh.
My friend and I got dresses from the same store but still mine is best than hers.
She gave bars of chocolate to everyone of us but sadly I got the smaller one of all the options available.

rules.title: Confusing verbs: fall/fell, rise/raise, lie/lay
rules.concept: Confusing verbs: fall–fell–fallen–falling means 'to fall' (intransitive), while fell–felled–felled–felling means 'to make something fall / cut down' (transitive). Rise–rose–risen–rising means 'to get up, increase or grow' (intransitive), while raise–raised–raised–raising means 'to lift, increase or bring up something' (transitive). Lie–lay–lain–lying means 'to recline or be lying down' (intransitive), while lay–laid–laid–laying means 'to lay something down or place something' (transitive).

examples.sentence: I knew I had sprained my ankle, the moment I felled.
Your favourite vase felled off the table during the earthquake.
Yash has raised as one of the top athletes in the entire state.
With temperatures on the rise, it's crucial to rise awareness about the pressing issue of global warming.
I was in a park when I felt sick, so I laid on a bench nearby.
She had lain the bag down before she left for the seminar.

rules.title: Verbs with identical V1/V2/V3 forms
rules.concept: These verbs have the same V1, V2 and V3 forms: wed, cost, set, bet, bid, thrust, hit, cut, slit, spread, read, burst, quit, shut, shed, cast, rid, telecast, broadcast, overcast, forecast, etc.

examples.sentence: After getting scolded by his father, he shutted the door and started studying.
Taylor Swift's new concert will be broadcasted live on radio and television.
He has already molten some gold to make a necklace for you so you should wait for some time.
People accuse him of stealing that necklace but the charges against him could not be proven in court.

rules.title: Stative Verbs take no progressive (-ing) form
rules.concept: Stative verbs are not used in the progressive (-ing) form. Examples: think, believe, consider, have, own, possess, look, seem, appear, consist, contain, comprise, feel, smell, taste, sound, know, resemble, like, love, want, agree, hate, forgive, forget, remember, depend, exist, etc.

examples.sentence: I am vaguely remembering that I met him during a concert.
Have you noticed that he is strongly resembling his brother in appearance?

rules.title: No 'as' after certain verbs
rules.concept: Do not use 'as' after these verbs: make, choose, elect, select, anoint, appoint, name, call, think, consider, etc.

examples.sentence: Although I met him only 5 months ago, I consider him as one of my closest friends.
He has been performing very well in last few matches, therefore the team has decided to make him as captain of the team.

rules.title: Active vs Passive voice based on the subject
rules.concept: If the subject is the doer of the action, use the active voice. If the subject is the receiver of the action, use the passive voice (be + third form of the verb). Example: 'My car was stolen by somebody' (subject is the receiver, so passive). Example: 'Somebody stole my car' (subject is the doer, so active).

examples.sentence: The wounded woman was treating by the doctor at the hospital.
examples.correction: Use 'was being treated' instead of 'was treating'.

examples.sentence: While playing in the park some children were being teased the animals.
examples.correction: Use 'were teasing' instead of 'were being teased'.

rules.title: Used to / be used to
rules.concept: 'Used to + base form of the verb' expresses a past habit. 'Be + used to + gerund' means to be accustomed to something (a habit of the past or the present). 'Be + used + infinitive' is passive and means 'to be used for the purpose of'.

examples.sentence: When I was a child, I used to playing cricket with my father every sunday.
I have worked at a call center for 7 years therefore I am used to work in night shifts also.
examples.correction: Use 'working' instead of 'working' (as printed in the source).

examples.sentence: The police inspector told my father that my stolen car was used to carrying some illegal drugs to Gujrat.

rules.title: Need and Dare as marginal auxiliaries
rules.concept: 'Need' and 'Dare' are marginal auxiliary verbs. They act as modals in these structures: (1) 'need not' and 'dare not'; (2) WH-word + need/dare + subject + main verb + ? As modals they are followed by the base form of the verb without 'to'.

examples.sentence: You need not to worry about this mole as it's totally benign.
How dare you to say these words to my father?
You do not need pay anything as all these bills are covered under the insurance.
examples.correction: Use 'do not need to pay' or 'need not pay' instead of 'do not need pay'.

rules.title: Can, May, Could, Might
rules.concept: 'Can' expresses ability, an informal request, and negative possibility. 'May' expresses a polite request and both positive and negative possibility. 'Could' expresses a polite request, remote possibility, and is the past of 'can'. 'Might' expresses less possibility and is the past of 'may'.

examples.sentence: We should let Shruti handle international clients as she may speak several languages.
I have forgotten my phone at home, will I use yours to call home and call someone to pick me up.
May you come with me to the clinic as I am too weak to drive right now.
He told me that he may join Aman's batch to prepare for competitive exams.

rules.title: Would, Ought to, Should, Must
rules.concept: 'Would' expresses a polite request, a past habit, and is the past of 'will'. 'Ought to' gives moral advice. 'Should' gives general advice. 'Must' expresses obligation and very high possibility.

examples.sentence: When I was a child, I would hide under the bed to scare my parents.
If you earn a decent amount of income, you dare help the poor.
If you want to lose weight, You may stop eating fast food.
I feel that one could love one's country.

rules.title: Uncountable nouns: no article, number, or plural marker
rules.concept: Do not use a, an, one, two, these, those, many, or -s/-es with these nouns: (a) nouns that act like material nouns: bread, soap, shampoo, sand, iron, paper, hair, brick, food, grass, garbage, filth, etc.; (b) nouns that act like abstract nouns: scenery, machinery, jewellery, cutlery, crockery, stationery, luggage, baggage, money, evidence, equipment, furniture, advice, work, music, information, knowledge, wealth, etc.; (c) others: business, research, abuse, percentage, alphabet.

examples.sentence: Our NGO helps the people who live in slums and collect garbages for a living.
All the houses in our colony were destroyed during the earthquake except hers, because it was made of best quality bricks.
The scientists had all the equipments that they need in order to complete the experiment.
Thousands of tourists visit Jammu and Kashmir every year to see the beautiful sceneries.

rules.title: Nouns that look plural but are singular
rules.concept: These nouns look plural but are singular: (a) Some subject names: Physics, Mathematics, Economics, Politics etc. (b) Some game names: Billiards, Darts, Athletics, Dominoes etc. (c) Disease names: Rickets, Measles, Mumps, Diabetes, Rabies, Shingles. (d) Others: Innings, News, Summons etc.

examples.sentence: Mathematics are one of the subjects which I have found very difficult since school.
Darts are a form of throwing game where darts are thrown at a circular target.
The news of her getting that promotion were the reason behind that big smile on her face.
Rickets cause problems in the normal calcification of the growing bones.

rules.title: Nouns that are always used as plural
rules.concept: Some nouns are used as plural nouns: (a) Things that always exist in a pair: Scissors, Tongs, Pliers, Pincers, Bellows, Trousers, Pants, Pyjamas, Shorts, Fangs, Spectacles, Glasses, Opticals, Binoculars, Scales, Gallows, Fetters, Shackles. (b) Compliments, Thanks, Congratulations, Regards. (c) Valuables, Eatables, Belongings, Goods, Surroundings, Movables. (d) Ashes, Embers, Remains, Ruins, Proceedings, Clothes, Outskirts, Arrears, Dues, Sweets, Alms, Riches, Earnings, Savings, Proceeds, Odds.

examples.sentence: The binoculars was not in focus so he raised them and adjusted the focus.
Tongs is used by my grandmother to make chapatis.
All his goods was packed in some cardboard boxes when he was moving to another city.
The outskirts of the city has some good hospitals for the people living there.

rules.title: Nouns that look singular but are plural
rules.concept: Some nouns look singular but are plural: Cattle, Vermin, Police, Gentry, Peasantry, Children, People, Poultry, Cavalry, Clergy, Infantry etc.

examples.sentence: Do you know that cattle was considered wealth in ancient times?
Poultry is domesticated birds kept by humans for the purpose of harvesting animal products such as meat, eggs or feathers.
The police was informed by the locals about the dead body found near the lake.
Although they want to yet most people doesn't do exercise daily.

rules.title: Nouns with the same singular and plural forms
rules.concept: Some nouns have the same singular and plural forms: Deer, Sheep, Fish, Species, Series, Aircraft, Vacation, Offspring, Issue, Whereabouts, Headquarters, Wages, Means etc. Notes: 'Wages' meaning income/salary takes a plural verb; 'Wages' meaning result/outcome takes a singular or plural verb according to the meaning. 'Means' meaning income/resources takes a plural verb; 'Means' meaning channel/medium takes a singular or plural verb according to the meaning.

examples.sentence: When I went to Japan, I saw the remains of some aircrafts which attacked Japan amid world war 2.
Two series of lectures is scheduled for the coming week.
The wages of the workers was increased after they protested for 2 days.
The wages of burning midnight oil are always worth it.
His means is not enough to support such a large family.
Various means was used by them in order to communicate with their family stuck in Ukraine war.
Both of his brother in laws live in Agra and run a book shop there.
examples.correction: Use 'brothers in law' instead of 'brother in laws'.

examples.sentence: All the man teachers were called by the principal to his office yesterday.
Some passer bys saw the accident and stopped to help him when his car collided with a truck.
She gulped down two mouthsful of coffee before the meeting to remain awake.

rules.title: Apostrophe with Joint Possession and Pronouns
rules.concept: When two nouns share possession of the same thing and are joined by 'and', add the apostrophe ('s) only to the latter noun. The apostrophe ('s) can also be used with certain pronouns, e.g. everybody, somebody, nobody, everyone, someone, one. If a word already ends in an 'sh'/'s' sound, add only the apostrophe (') and not ('s).

examples.sentence: David's and Mindy's car has stopped functioning properly so they are thinking about selling it.
Your parents's trust on you has degraded because you kept on repeating the same mistakes.
The recent earthquake has destroyed everyone's house in our society.
For god sake , please forgive me. I promise that I won't repeat this mistake.

rules.title: Possessive Case of Compound Nouns
rules.concept: While forming the possessive case of a compound noun, place the apostrophe ('s) at the end of the whole compound.

examples.sentence: We get discount at that hospital because my son's in law sister works there.
examples.correction: Use 'son in law's' instead of 'son's in law'.

examples.sentence: When I married Anjali, I took over my father's in law business as he had no son.
examples.correction: Use 'father in law's' instead of 'father's in law'.

rules.title: Apostrophe with Non-Living Things
rules.concept: The apostrophe ('s) can be used with certain non-living things: Personification - sun's fury, death's icy hands, nature's law, country's honour, fortune's favourite, etc.; Dignified objects - court's order, duty's call, etc.; Celestial bodies - earth's atmosphere, sun's axis, etc.; Expressions of time, weight, value and distance - a ton's weight, 2 metres' gap, razor's edge, a pound's worth, etc.; Idioms - at a stone's throw, at one's wit's end, nature's call, etc.

examples.sentence: The temperature has touched 50°c in many areas this summer, I think no one will be saved from sun's fury this time.
Mohit has received a court's order barring him from entering the hotel.
After the rise of greenhouse gases the experts have noticed changes in Earth's atmosphere.
We sat at a 2 meter's gap from each other in that conference hall.
This resort is expensive because it is at a stone's throw from the famous beach.

rules.title: Adjective vs Adverb (Linking Verbs)
rules.concept: Use an adjective after a linking verb and an adverb after an action verb. Common linking verbs: be forms, become, get, grow, feel, smell, taste, sound, keep, remain, prove, look, seem, appear, etc.

examples.sentence: She behaved very rude with Ajay's parents so he stopped talking to her.
He got really madly when he saw his girlfriend having dinner with his friend.
Although she is a very impatient person yet she kept calmly during the interrogation.
I want to shift from this area because I don't feel safely here.

rules.title: Words with Identical Adjective and Adverb Forms
rules.concept: These words have the same adjective and adverb forms: fast, hard, late, straight, daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, etc. Hard (adjective) means tough; hard (adverb) means forcefully or with great effort; hardly (adverb) means scarcely or almost not at all. Also note: 'every day' is an adverb of frequency, while 'everyday' is an adjective.

examples.sentence: We have to make some choices hard in life if we want to be successful.
Reeta came home lately as she got stuck in the traffic while coming back from her office.
Shruti had to take an every day appointment with a therapist after she got diagnosed with clinical depression.
examples.correction: Use 'appointment every day' instead of 'every day appointment', because 'every day' is an adverb of frequency while 'everyday' is an adjective.

examples.sentence: After getting irritated by his friend's continuous sarcastic remarks, Yash told him straightly to stop bothering him anymore.

rules.title: Words Ending in -ly That Are Adjectives Only
rules.concept: These words are adjectives, not adverbs: godly, kingly, queenly, fatherly, motherly, brotherly, friendly, manly, womanly, miserly, niggardly, lively, lovely, deadly, cowardly, etc. Note the difference: nice (adjective) + ly = nicely (adverb), but man (noun) + ly = manly (adjective).

examples.sentence: The old lady in our neighbourhood is a very kind woman and she always treats me motherly.
examples.correction: Use 'like a mother' or 'in a motherly manner' instead of 'motherly'.

examples.sentence: He started his career as a sports commentator as he has a very deep and manly voice.
Army is for brave people and not for those who act cowardly as soon as they come across some danger.
examples.correction: Use 'like a coward' or 'in a cowardly manner' instead of 'cowardly'.

examples.sentence: We have stopped going out with Rajesh because he always acts miserly.
examples.correction: Use 'like a miser' or 'in a miserly manner' instead of 'miserly'.

rules.title: Position of adverbs of frequency
rules.concept: Position of adverbs of frequency: (1) Indefinite adverbs of frequency (often, seldom, always, rarely, never, etc.) are placed before the main verb. (2) Definite adverbs of frequency (daily, weekly, monthly, yearly, etc.) are placed at the end of the clause. (3) Some adverbs can occupy both positions: regularly, frequently, occasionally, etc.

examples.sentence: With the increasing work load and responsibilities, I have rarely time to continue my passion for painting.
examples.correction: Use 'I rarely have' instead of 'I have rarely'.

examples.sentence: He is physically strong and has a good health because he daily goes to the gym.
examples.correction: Use 'he goes to the gym daily' instead of 'he daily goes to the gym'.

rules.title: Too much vs much too; still vs yet
rules.concept: 'Too much' functions as an adjective, while 'much too' functions as an adverb. 'Still' is used with continuous tenses and is placed before the verb (except with linking verbs). 'Yet' is used in negative sentences, generally with the present perfect tense, and is placed after the verb (if intransitive) or after the object (if the verb is transitive).

examples.sentence: His teachers were too much angry with him for coming late to school and failing all the classes.
I think that you have spent much too money on you suit.
He cannot come to the office for a few more weeks because he is yet recovering from his illness.
Rohini didn't attend the book club meeting yesterday because she hasn't still finished reading the book.

rules.title: Inversion
rules.concept: Inversion structures: Adverb + helping verb + subject + main verb. With an adverb of place: Adverb of place + main verb + subject.

examples.sentence: Barely she had got back in bed when her alarm went off.
Never I have encountered such rudeness before I stared working in this office.
examples.correction: Use 'Never have I' in place of 'Never I have'.

examples.sentence: Just two meters away from their house was lying 3 dead bodies.
When I told them my plan, Rajesh joined me and so kunal did.
examples.correction: Use 'so did Kunal' instead of 'so Kunal did'.

rules.title: Usage of articles: a/an vs the
rules.concept: Usage of articles: 'a/an' is used for a non-specific or indefinite noun, whereas 'the' is used for a specific or already identified noun.

examples.sentence: I was happy to see a fireman who saved my life when my house got on fire.
I can't believe that he lives in the small flat in Pacific golf society.
examples.correction: Use 'in a small' instead of 'in the small'.

examples.sentence: My uncle gifted me the expensive watch on my 18th birthday.
A man whom we met while we were coming back is brother in law.

rules.title: Articles: a vs an
rules.concept: The choice between 'a' and 'an' depends on sound, not spelling. Some words begin with a vowel letter but have a consonant sound: unit, unique, utopia, universal, uniform, useful, union, university, European, eulogy, one, etc. — these take 'a'. Some words begin with a consonant letter but have a vowel sound: hour, heir, heiress, honest, honour, honorary, SMS, RTI, MNC, LLB (and abbreviations beginning with F, H, L, M, N, S, R, X) — these take 'an'.

examples.sentence: My brother is an interesting boy who has an unique sense of humour.
If you try to blackmail me again, I will not hesitate in lodging a FIR against you.
The spammer sent him a SMS saying that all his bank accounts would get blocked soon.
They awarded him a honorary degree for his tremendous work in the field of cinema.

rules.title: Proper noun used as a common noun
rules.concept: When a proper noun is used as a common noun, an article can be used with it.

examples.sentence: The infamous criminal Joe adams is also known as Robin Hood of his area because he looted from the rich and gave it to the poor.
examples.correction: Use 'as the Robin Hood' instead of 'as Robin Hood'.

examples.sentence: You should probably give up on your dream of becoming a cricketer and accept the fact that you are not Sachin.

rules.title: Omission of articles
rules.concept: Do not use any article with these places when they are used for their primary purpose: school, university, college, hospital, church, temple, jail, prison, market, bed, etc. Also do not use any article with the names of games, days, months, colours, seasons, festivals, subjects, languages, cities, continents, lakes, diseases, meals, etc.

examples.sentence: I know that you don't earn much but you should try to send your children to the school.
After a long and tedious day, Yamini came home and went to the bed.
My brother and I always wait for the Christmas because it is filled with joy and sweet treats.
As soon as I get an opportunity, I will shift to the Australia.

rules.title: Verb agreement with the first noun
rules.concept: When two nouns are joined by these words, the verb agrees with the first noun: between, with, along with, but, together with, including, excluding, except, like, unlike, followed by, accompanied by, in addition to, besides, and not, but not, as well as, etc.

examples.sentence: The prime minister accompanied by his bodyguards come to the red fort every year to hoist the flag on Republic day.
All the languages besides Hindi is spoken by the new student who got transferred from Korea last week.

rules.title: Each / Either / Neither and Each / Every
rules.concept: Each/Either/Neither + of + plural noun takes a singular verb. Each/Either/Neither + singular noun takes a singular verb. Each/Every + singular noun + and + each/every + singular noun takes a singular verb.

examples.sentence: Each of my cats were fed by my neighbour when I was out of town for a meeting.
Each chapter of the newly launched book are interesting but the last one was spectacular.
Every girl and every boy were given a packet of sweets on independence day at school.

rules.title: One of + plural noun; The + adjective as subject
rules.concept: One + of + plural noun takes a singular verb. 'The' + adjective used as a subject takes a plural verb.

examples.sentence: I got all my furniture at a discounted price because one of my friends own a furniture shop.
The rich always looks down on the poor, and don't treat them with kindness.

rules.title: Articles before joined nouns indicating same or different persons
rules.concept: Article + noun and article + noun refers to two different people (plural verb). Article + noun and noun (article used only once) refers to the same person (singular verb).

examples.sentence: The host and hostess /of the party were very nice and /they welcomed each guest with/ a big smile on their faces.
The Principal and the secretary/ of our school is coming and many/ arrangements were made by the /teachers for their visit.
The Vice-President and the chairman/ of the Rajya Sabha is elected/ by an electoral college consisting of members of /both Houses of Parliament.

rules.title: Gerunds and infinitives as subject
rules.concept: Use a singular verb when gerunds or infinitives are used as the subject.

examples.sentence: Writing poems have been my hobby since I was in school.
To give suggestions are easy, when you are not the one in that particular situation.

rules.title: Either–or / Neither–nor / Not only–but also
rules.concept: With either–or, neither–nor and not only–but also, the verb agrees with the noun or pronoun nearest to it.

examples.sentence: Neither Shruti nor her friends is going to attend the convocation on Saturday at the university.
Either Ashish or his colleagues is responsible for leaking the confidential information about the products of the company.
Not only my parents but also my brother are coming to my destination wedding in goa.

rules.title: Many / Many a / A great many
rules.concept: Many + plural noun takes a plural verb. Many a + singular noun takes a singular verb. A great/good many + plural noun takes a plural verb.

examples.sentence: Many aspirants preparing for this exam was shocked when they found that the exam got cancelled.
Many a man have tried to climb Mount Everest without oxygen cylinder but most of them failed to do so.
A great many lives was saved by the rescue team during the tsunami of 2004.

rules.title: A number of / The number of
rules.concept: A number of + plural noun takes a plural verb. The number of + plural noun takes a singular verb.

examples.sentence: A number of players of our team is still injured from the last game, therefore we can't play today's match.
The number of employees who are getting laid off by tech companies are increasing every year.

rules.title: Collective nouns and 'none of'
rules.concept: A collective noun normally takes a singular verb, but takes a plural verb if there is a hint of referring to its individual members. None + of + plural noun takes a singular verb.

examples.sentence: The committee have agreed to build a park for all the people living in the society.
The jury has different opinions about the case of a mother killing a man to save her child.
None of his friends were present at his funeral.

rules.title: Proper Noun as Subject
rules.concept: When a proper noun is used as the subject, a singular verb is used.

examples.sentence: The harry potter series were written by J.K. Rowling and is very popular among teenagers and young adults.
Mathematics have always been my favourite subject since childhood.
I have seen him using a calculator even for basic calculations so I think that his mathematics is very weak.
Abhishek does not took bus to school everyday because his father drops him while going to work.
His parents got a call from the school because he did not went to school yesterday.
Trisha is play chess with her friends in her room while her younger brother is watching them from a distance.
The young writer Brian Wiest has already wrote three books and he is working on another one.
Shreya was nervous to go to her rich friend's birthday party because she had not ate at such an expensive restaurant before.
She has been worked on this report since eight o'clock this morning.
I am teaching English for the last 10 years.
examples.correction: Use 'I have been teaching' instead of 'I am teaching'.

examples.sentence: Shruti is working as a content writer since 2022.
examples.correction: Use 'has been working' instead of 'is working'.

examples.sentence: Mrs. Sharma knows the neighbourhood better than anyone else, as she is living here for the last 20 years.
examples.correction: Use 'has been living here' instead of 'is living here'.

examples.sentence: I have been knowing her for the last 5 years.
examples.correction: Use 'have known' instead of 'have been knowing'.

examples.sentence: Nalini didn't call me even once since she moved to Australia.
examples.correction: Use 'has not called me' instead of "didn't call me".

rules.title: Hints of Present Indefinite and Present Continuous
rules.concept: Hints of Present Indefinite: proverbs, facts, and words such as always, often, daily, everyday, regularly, frequently, occasionally, seldom, never, etc. Hints of Present Continuous: at this time, at this moment, at present, currently, these days, right now, etc.

examples.sentence: As Rohan lives in mountains, he has often gone for a hike with his friends.
He is seldom leaving his home because he is an introvert.

rules.title: Hints of Present Perfect and Past Perfect Usage
rules.concept: Hints of Present Perfect: yet, so far, already, just, just now, lately, recently, of late, etc. Past Perfect usage: Past Perfect + before + Past Indefinite; Past Indefinite + after + Past Perfect.

examples.sentence: I hadn't got any email regarding the job interview yet.
Her children hadn't been well lately, so she is taking them to a doctor.
I never met anyone from India before I started living with my new roommate Sangeeta.
examples.correction: Use 'I had never met' instead of 'I never met'.

examples.sentence: The Doctor had arrived after the patient had died from a heart attack.

rules.title: Hints of Past Indefinite and Future Indefinite
rules.concept: Hints of Past Indefinite: yesterday, ago, in past, last day/Sunday/week/year, etc. Hints of Future Indefinite: tomorrow, next Sunday/week/month/year, coming days/Sunday/week/month/year, shortly, presently, in 2040 (future years), etc.

examples.sentence: It had rained cats and dogs yesterday, and many slums got flooded with water.
examples.correction: Use 'it rained' instead of 'It had rained'.

examples.sentence: I have gone to the cinema with my family last Sunday.
examples.correction: Use 'I went to' instead of 'I have gone to'.

examples.sentence: All the arrangements have been made for the party and the guests arrive shortly.
We gather more information in the coming days to determine our next step in the case.
examples.correction: Use 'We will gather' instead of 'We gather'.

rules.title: Tense agreement between main clause and sub-clause
rules.concept: If the main clause is in the past tense, the sub-clause should also be in the past tense. Do not use the future tense after these conjunctions: when, while, if, until, unless, provided that, as soon as, before, after, etc.

examples.sentence: My mother asked me where I am going.
examples.correction: Use 'I was going' instead of 'I am going'.

examples.sentence: The teacher wanted to know if the students have completed their homework.
I will call Shraddha when I will finish my presentation for tomorrow's meeting.
examples.correction: Use 'I finish' instead of 'I will finish'.

examples.sentence: You will get a seat in AC compartment only if someone will cancel his ticket.

rules.title: 'By the time' structures
rules.concept: Use the structure: Past Perfect + by the time + Past Indefinite. Use the structure: Future Perfect + by the time + Present Indefinite.

examples.sentence: Witnesses told the judge that the suspects already escaped from the back of the store by the time police officers arrived.
I finished all the household chores by the time my mother woke up.
By the time, You come back from market, I will complete my homework.
examples.correction: Use 'will have completed' instead of 'will complete'.

examples.sentence: He will have held that position for ten years by the time he will retire.

rules.title: Tense according to the meaning of the sentence
rules.concept: Use the correct tense according to the meaning of the sentence.

examples.sentence: My parents threw me a big surprise party and invite all of my best friends.
Most people bought groceries from the supermarket but we prefer our local shop.
I used to go to my grandparents house every summer when I was a kid and every morning we plucks flowers from their garden.
The judge asked the man if he has stolen five thousand rupees from the bag.
He started a very small business two years ago but it grew very fast as the country is experiencing a boom at that time.
Most children like to rest in the afternoon after they returned from school.

rules.title: Question tag basics
rules.concept: 1. A question tag contains a helping verb + a pronoun. 2. Positive sentences take negative question tags and vice versa. 3. Use the helping verb in its contracted form.

examples.sentence: We have already met each other, didn't we?
The trains in India never come on time, aren't they?
The new HR was late on his first day of job, weren't he?
An Aspirant should be consistent in his studies, don't he?
Let's go for a dinner for our anniversary, will we?
You haven't seen the film that I recommended to you last week, did you?

rules.title: Use 'they' in the question tag with indefinite subjects
rules.concept: If the following words are used as the subject of a statement, use 'they' in the question tag: each, either, neither, none, no one, everybody, nobody, anybody, everyone, anyone, all, any, etc.

examples.sentence: Everybody has come on time today, hasn't he?
None of his colleagues came to his retirement party, have they?
All of you were present there at the time of accident, weren't they?

rules.title: Correlative conjunctions join words of the same rank
rules.concept: These correlative conjunctions join words of the same rank (same grammatical category): either - or, not only - but also, neither - nor, both - and.

examples.sentence: You have a long weekend coming up, so either you can go for a vacation or stay at home.
The new teacher teaches them not only mathematics but also provides career counseling to them.
examples.correction: Remove 'not only' after 'them' and place 'not only' before 'teaches'.

examples.sentence: Both my friend as well as I like to watch hollywood movies in our free time.

rules.title: Hardly/Scarcely - when; No sooner - than
rules.concept: Correlative conjunction pairs: hardly/scarcely - when; no sooner - than.

examples.sentence: Hardly had I started having my breakfast than the bell rang.
Scarcely he had entered the office when everyone started laughing.
examples.correction: Use 'Scarcely had he' instead of 'Scarcely he had'.

examples.sentence: No sooner had the dance performance ended when the audience started cheering for the dancer.

rules.title: Correlative conjunction pairs: although/though–yet, so–as, as–as
rules.concept: Correlative conjunction pairs: 'although/though' is paired with 'yet' (not 'but'); 'so...as' is used in negative sentences; 'as...as' is used in positive and negative sentences.

examples.sentence: Though there were many people in the museum but there was pin drop silence.
Radhika is not so intelligent as she used to be in her 10th standard.
Shivam's car is so expensive as mine, but it has a lot more features.
examples.correction: Use 'as expensive as' instead of 'so expensive as'.

rules.title: Correlative conjunction pairs: so–that, too–to + V1
rules.concept: Correlative conjunction pairs: 'so' is paired with 'that'; 'too' is followed by 'to + first form of the verb'.

examples.sentence: The dumbbells were too heavy that he sprained his wrist while lifting them.
Aryan was too tired after the party that he couldn't attend his class the next day.
His marks in 12th class were so low to get admission in a good college.
He was so old to walk on his own therefore he had to carry a cane with him all the time.

rules.title: Correlative conjunction pairs: between–and, lest–should
rules.concept: Correlative conjunction pairs: 'between' is paired with 'and' (not 'to'); 'lest' is followed by 'should'.

examples.sentence: The British Raj was the period of British Parliament rule on the Indian subcontinent between 1858 to 1947.
The award function has started and the chief guest will arrive between 9pm to 10pm.
Study for 10 hours daily, lest you will fail your medical entrance exam.

rules.title: Correlative conjunction pairs: such–as, such–that
rules.concept: 'Such...as' is used when 'as' functions as a relative pronoun (meaning 'who/which'). 'Such...that' is used when 'that' functions as a conjunction (expressing result).

examples.sentence: I like teaching only such students who are serious about their career.
She is such a bad-tempered person as no one can live with her for long.
It was such a ferocious and brutal animal as everyone preferred to stay away from its cage at the zoo.

rules.title: Do not use 'so' with 'as'; do not use 'that' before why/how/where/when/what
rules.concept: Do not use the conjunction 'so' if the conjunction 'as' has already been used. Do not use the conjunction 'that' when it is followed by the conjunctions why, how, where, when or what.

examples.sentence: As I have lived in Mumbai for a year so, I know how expensive it is.
When Shreya was leaving home last night, I asked her that where she was going but she didn't reply and left.
Radhika's husband asked her that what she was doing.

rules.title: Until vs unless; no 'not' with unless/until
rules.concept: 'Until' is used for time, while 'unless' is used for a general condition. Do not use 'not' together with the conjunctions 'unless' or 'until' in the same clause.

examples.sentence: Until you control your diet, you won't be able to lose fat.
Please promise me that you will wait for me here unless I return.
Yash will not go on the trip unless he does not have enough money for that.

rules.title: 'Reason...that' not 'reason...because'; do not use 'supposing' with 'if'
rules.concept: If the noun 'reason' is used in a sentence, do not use the conjunction 'because'; use 'that' instead. Do not use the conjunctions 'supposing' and 'if' together.

examples.sentence: The reason she is upset these days is because she broke up with her boyfriend.
The reason Payal could not attend the meeting was because she had a severe headache.
Supposing if you are wrong, will you apologise for all this?
examples.correction: Only one of the two conjunctions should be used — either 'supposing' or 'if'.

rules.title: Use the correct conjunction according to the meaning of the sentence
rules.concept: Use the correct conjunction according to the meaning of the sentence: as, because, since, so, therefore, although, though, but, yet, so that, if, whether, when, while, etc.

examples.sentence: He has all the required skills and lots of money and he dare not start a company.
She wouldn't have suffered when you had helped her in time.
He has very little money in his account so he offered to help her for her treatment.
Her husband was very loving and caring although she left him.
Yamini broke my laptop but I asked her to get it repaired.
I missed my bus as I had to book a taxi to the office.

rules.title: Verbs that take no preposition
rules.concept: Do not use a preposition after these verbs: Meet, Join, Obey, Violate, Ask, Kid, Tell, Inform, Remind, Warn, Thank, Advise, Reach, Resist, Resemble, Attack, Afford, Demand, Comprise, Investigate, Enter, Flee, Explain, Describe, Discuss, Disobey, Order, Stress, Emphasize, Await, Despise, etc.

examples.sentence: The play that we are going to perform in the annual event, comprises of total 3 acts.
Juhi strongly resembles of her Grandmother in appearance and in temperament.
The police are investigating into the murder of the man whose body was found on the highway this morning.
Let's discuss about your current situation and try to find a solution.

rules.title: Use of 'to' before an indirect object
rules.concept: Do not use the preposition 'to' after these verbs when they are followed by an indirect object (a person): Ask, Beg, Inform, Advise, Allow, Call, Assure, Apprise, Remind, Warn, Thank, Wish, Order, Request, Invite, Forbade, Welcome, Congratulate, Compliment, etc. Do use the preposition 'to' after these verbs when they are followed by an indirect object: Propose, Announce, Apologize, Plead, Talk, Report, Suggest, Spoke, Listen, Wrote, Pray, Complain, Describe, Explain, Appeal, etc.

examples.sentence: Whenever I visit dominos I always ask to the cook to put extra sauce on my pizza.
I want to thank to Reeta for letting me stay at her place when I first came to Mumbai and had no place to go.
I was upset because my parents forbade to me from going to the school trip.
I apologized my client for cancelling the meeting at such a short notice.
He proposed his parents that they should go for a family vacation in Kerala.
When my grandfather died I asked the doctor to explain me the cause of his death.

rules.title: Conjunctions vs prepositions: because / in case / unless
rules.concept: 'Because' is a conjunction while 'because of' is a preposition. 'In case' is a conjunction while 'in case of' is a preposition. 'Unless' is a conjunction while 'without' is a preposition. A conjunction is followed by a clause; a preposition is followed by a noun or noun phrase.

examples.sentence: The semi finale of T20 world cup was stopped because the heavy rain.
I love the spring season, because of the blossoming flowers and the green leaves fill my heart with joy.
Everyone bought groceries in bulk during covid in case of the lockdown gets extended.
examples.correction: Use 'in case' instead of 'in case of'.

examples.sentence: You can call me anytime in case any emergency.
examples.correction: Use 'in case of' instead of 'in case'.

rules.title: Instead of / In spite of / Despite
rules.concept: 'Instead of' means 'in place of' (as an alternative). 'In spite of' and 'Despite' both mean 'notwithstanding' or 'even though'. 'Despite' is never followed by 'of'.

examples.sentence: Inspite of buying a new car, I decided to use my father's old vintage car.
examples.correction: Use 'instead of' instead of 'in spite of'.

examples.sentence: Instead of the financial difficulties, they never borrowed any money from family or friends.
examples.correction: Use 'in spite of' instead of 'instead of'.

examples.sentence: Despite of facing a lot of criticism, Tobey continued his struggle of becoming an actor.

rules.title: Different prepositions with nouns joined by 'and'
rules.concept: If two nouns are joined by the conjunction 'and' and they do not take the same preposition, the appropriate different prepositions must be used with each noun.

examples.sentence: It is clear that my bag is superior but cheaper than yours.
Once I hand over the keys to you, I won't be liable for any loss and damage to this car.

rules.title: Among vs Between
rules.concept: 'Between' is used for two persons or things, while 'among' is used for more than two. Note: 'Between' can be used for more than two when there is a relationship between the individual elements.

examples.sentence: My mother stood among me and my brother and told us to stop fighting with each other.
The railway authority warned us to keep our belongings safe as there could be pickpockets between the passengers.
A new peace agreement has been signed among India, China, Pakistan and Sri lanka.

rules.title: Angry/Annoyed/Vexed/Disgusted + at/with
rules.concept: Use 'at' with angry / annoyed / vexed / disgusted when referring to a thing, and 'with' when referring to a person.

examples.sentence: I was angry at my mother for not telling me about her disease earlier.
I was angry with my new phone's performance because it stopped working when I needed it the most.

rules.title: Supply + prepositions
rules.concept: Use the correct pattern with 'supply': supply something TO somebody; supply somebody WITH something; supply something FOR a purpose.

examples.sentence: Shruti started a new business with her brother in which she supplies stationery with all the schools in her town.
examples.correction: Use 'stationery to all' instead of 'stationery with all'.

examples.sentence: When my brother was quarantined during covid outbreak, I supplied him to food and medicines.
I supply medicines to homeless people to their treatment.

rules.title: Fixed prepositions
rules.concept: Learn these fixed preposition combinations: accused of, cope with, dispose of, afraid of, different from.

examples.sentence: Rohan was accused for theft and fraud by the company he was working in.
She has not been coming to office for a week because she is still coping up with her mother's death.
examples.correction: Use 'coping with' instead of 'coping up with'.

examples.sentence: You should dispose off all the extra items that you have not used in the last 2 years.
Neha cannot go to the jungle for camping as she is afraid from wild animals.
Your curry tastes different than the one we had at your mother's house.

rules.title: Infinitive describing a noun or pronoun
rules.concept: If an infinitive is used to describe a noun or a pronoun, that noun or pronoun must be the object of the verb used in the infinitive. If it is not, add the necessary preposition after the infinitive.

examples.sentence: Sudhir was upset about losing his job but he had no one to talk.
He lives with his parents because he has several health problems and needs someone to rely.

rules.title: Present Participle (V1+ing): wrong subject of reference
rules.concept: A present participle phrase (V1+ing) must refer to the correct subject of the main clause. If the subject does not match, rewrite the phrase with the proper subject and verb (e.g. 'While he was ...').

examples.sentence: Walking in the park, a snake bit him.
examples.correction: Use 'While he was' before 'Walking in the park'.

examples.sentence: Walking down the road, a car caught Rohit's attention.
examples.correction: Use 'While he was' before 'Walking down the road'.

examples.sentence: Climbing the mountain, different types of animals were seen by the hikers.
examples.correction: Use 'While they were' before 'Climbing the mountain,'.

examples.sentence: Travelling through the metro, her mobile went missing.

rules.title: Present Participle (V1+ing): wrong subject of reference
rules.concept: A present participle phrase (V1+ing) must have the correct subject of reference; insert the appropriate pronoun before the participle when the subject is wrong.

examples.sentence: Being injured, we took him to hospital.
Being hospitalized, Radhika's parents took good care of her.
Being strong, his mother called him to help with all the lifting while shifting to a new place.
Being sick for 3 days during covid, Sanjana told her roommate to quarantine herself.

rules.title: Perfect Participle (Having + V3)
rules.concept: When one action is completed before another, use the perfect participle 'Having + V3' (or 'After + V1+ing') instead of the simple present participle. Use 'Having been + V3' when the subject is the receiver of the action.

examples.sentence: Having played for 2 hours, he went home.
Completing the assignment, Suhani lay on the sofa to rest.
Sleeping for 2 hours, she woke up and started the work again.
Having caught, the thief admitted stealing a woman's purse in the train.
examples.correction: Use 'Having been caught' instead of 'Having caught'.

rules.title: Gerund or noun after certain phrases and adjectives
rules.concept: Use a gerund (V1+ing) or a noun after these phrases and adjectives: look forward to, with a view to, in addition to, pay attention to, conducive to, accustomed to, prone to, vulnerable to, addicted to, devoted to, indifferent to, object to, averse to, opposed to, prefer to, etc.

examples.sentence: All of us are looking forward to join his new company.
He was not accustomed to work at night therefore he felt uncomfortable here.
I prefer watching Hollywood movies than reading novels.

rules.title: Verbs followed by infinitives vs gerunds
rules.concept: Verbs followed by infinitives: seem, appear, decide, desire, want, try, endeavour, stop, hurry, fail, happen, refuse, forget, remember, promise, prove. For example, 'I want to watch a movie' (correct: watch), while 'I enjoy watching Hollywood movies' (correct: watching). Verbs followed by gerunds: detest, mind, resent, avoid, stop, excuse, resist, miss, prevent, defer, delay, postpone, consider, appreciate, admire, forget, forgive, recollect, remember, suggest, risk, engage, admit, propose, etc.

examples.sentence: He decided going on a trip to Manali with his family during his winter vacation.
She failed meeting the deadline of submitting the assignment and got zero marks.

rules.title: Verbs followed by gerund (V-ing)
rules.concept: Certain verbs such as forget, detest, avoid and consider are followed by a gerund (V-ing) rather than an infinitive. (Concept heading not present in this chunk; examples 339-342 continue from the previous page.)

examples.sentence: Shruti was tensed because she forgot bringing her laptop to the meeting.
Satvik leaves for the airports hours before his flight because he detests to wait in long queues.
She avoids to eat junk food since she got diagnosed with stomach ulcers.
After getting fired from her job, she's considering to follow her dream of becoming a dancer.

rules.title: Bare infinitive after certain verbs
rules.concept: Use the bare infinitive (verb without 'to') after these verbs: let, bid, make, see, notice, feel, hear, smell, have, watch, help, etc.

examples.sentence: She lets his brother to borrow her car whenever he needs to go to work.
We heard him to say very mean things about your wife and parents.
We saw him to cross the road with his children.

rules.title: Causative verbs: make, have, get
rules.concept: Causative structures: 'make' and 'have' take a bare infinitive when followed by a person doing the action (make/have + object + V1), while 'have' and 'get' take the past participle (V3) when the object is a thing that receives the action (have/get + object + V3). (No rule text was printed for this concept in the chunk; the pattern is shown through the examples.)

examples.sentence: The coach made the players to practise every day for the upcoming championship.
The director had the actors rehearsed their lines thoroughly before starting the shoot.
Ranjan had the cook prepared a special meal for the guests at his birthday party.
Anaya got her car to repair by the mechanic after it broke down on the highway.
The chef had the food tasting by his assistants before serving it to the guests.
I got my presentation to review by my supervisor before the meeting to ensure it had no errors.

rules.title: Conditional sentences
rules.concept: Conditional sentence patterns: do not use 'will' in the 'if' clause; in the second conditional use 'were' instead of 'was'; and in the third conditional (if + had + V3) the main clause takes a perfect modal form such as 'might have + V3'. (No rule text was printed for this concept in the chunk; the pattern is shown through the examples.)

examples.sentence: If you will finish the project on time, the boss will definitely consider giving you a promotion.
If I was the president of the USA, I would surely help the poor countries of Africa.
If Abhishek had completed his degree in engineering, they might hire him.
examples.correction: Use 'might have hired' instead of 'might hire'.

rules.title: Mixed conditionals
rules.concept: Mixed conditionals: when the imagined condition refers to a permanent or present state, use 'were' in the if-clause instead of 'had been'; when the condition is in the past but the result refers to the present, the main clause takes a present form such as 'could be' rather than 'could have been'. (No rule text was printed for this concept in the chunk; the pattern is shown through the examples.)

examples.sentence: If I had been his father, I would have taught him a lesson for his indecent behaviour.
If she had been from the USA, she would have got opportunities that she deserved.
If Juhi had asked her classmates for help that day, she could have been alive today.

rules.title: 'I wish' structures
